title: Matthew Weiner Departs Eddie Murphy’s ‘The Chairman’ Series as Showrunner, Deadline Reports
body:
The high‑profile Peacock drama starring Eddie Murphy, “The Chairman,” has lost its original showrunner and writer, veteran television creator Matthew Weiner, who announced his departure this week. The series, which was billed as a “Mad Men” alumnus teaming up with Murphy for a corporate‑politics thriller, will now search for a new showrunner to steer the project forward, according to insiders familiar with the development.

Weiner, best known for creating and helming the critically acclaimed “Mad Men,” was tapped in early 2023 to serve as writer, executive producer and showrunner for “The Chairman.” The series, set to explore the machinations of a powerful media mogul, promised a blend of Weiner’s signature period‑drama sensibility with Murphy’s comic timing and star power. However, sources say that creative differences and scheduling conflicts led to an amicable split, with the “Mad Men” creator stepping away before the series entered production. “He remains supportive of the project and is eager to see it succeed under new leadership,” a representative for the production company said.

The exit of a showrunner at this stage is not unprecedented in today’s television landscape, but it does raise questions about the future tone and direction of “The Chairman.” Weiner’s involvement had been a major selling point, positioning the series as a prestige drama capable of attracting both critical acclaim and a broad audience. Without his guiding hand, the production will need to find a successor who can balance the show’s ambitious narrative scope with Murphy’s comedic strengths. Industry observers suggest that the search may focus on writers who have experience navigating high‑stakes corporate storylines while maintaining a character‑driven focus—qualities that defined both “Mad Men” and recent successful dramas such as “Succession.”

The timing of the change also coincides with a broader shift in the streaming market, where networks are increasingly cautious about large‑scale, star‑driven projects amid tightening budgets. Peacock, which has been positioning itself as a home for original, high‑budget content, will likely scrutinize the budget and schedule for “The Chairman” as it appoints a new showrunner. The platform’s recent slate includes a mix of limited series and anthology formats, suggesting that the network may consider re‑structuring the series into a more compact format if it deems that a better fit for its current strategy.

For Eddie Murphy, the development hiccup is a reminder of the challenges that come with transitioning from film and stand‑up comedy to leading a serialized drama. Murphy’s last major television venture, the sitcom “The Kids Are Alright,” ran for two seasons, but “The Chairman” was expected to showcase a different facet of his talent. In a brief statement, Murphy expressed confidence in the project’s potential, saying, “I’m excited about the story we’re telling and look forward to bringing it to life with a great team.” His commitment suggests that the series will continue moving forward despite the leadership change.

As the production gears up to hire a new showrunner, attention will turn to how the creative vision evolves and whether the series can maintain its momentum without Weiner’s imprint. The next few weeks are likely to bring announcements regarding the incoming showrunner and possibly adjustments to the show’s structure or episode count. If the new leadership can harness Murphy’s charisma while delivering the intricate, character‑driven storytelling that audiences have come to expect from prestige dramas, “The Chairman” could still emerge as a flagship series for Peacock. Until then, the industry will watch closely to see how this high‑profile collaboration reshapes itself in the wake of a notable creative departure.
